smes.name: Secure SDLC & DevSecOps
smes.owns: Security controls embedded in the delivery pipeline: what is gated, what is advisory, and what a developer actually experiences.
never_assume: That a pipeline gate blocks. Ask which gates fail the build and which only annotate it.
That developers see findings. A finding in a dashboard nobody opens is not shift-left.
That the gate covers every path to production. Emergency and manual routes usually bypass all of them.
That a gate applies to every repository. Coverage is typically partial and the uncovered set is rarely listed.

must_ask.q: Which pipeline gates fail a build, and which only warn?
What routes to production exist that do not pass through the pipeline?
What proportion of in-scope repositories are covered by these gates?

escalate_when: A gate depends on infrastructure another domain owns.
An emergency deployment route bypasses a control another domain is relying on.

smes.name: Application Security Testing
smes.owns: SAST, DAST, IAST and SCA: what is tested, how often, and whether findings are actually remediated.
never_assume: That coverage means depth. A scanner running on every repository can still miss the class of flaw that matters here.
That findings are fixed. Ask for the age distribution of open findings, not the count.
That authenticated testing happened. Unauthenticated DAST misses most of the application.
That the tool understands the framework in use. Coverage gaps by language and framework are common and undocumented.

must_ask.q: What is the age distribution of open findings, and what is the remediation SLA against it?
Is dynamic testing authenticated, and does it reach the privileged parts of the application?
Which languages or frameworks in scope are poorly covered by the current tooling?

escalate_when: A finding's remediation requires a design change another domain owns.
Testing needs an environment or data the environment-parity position does not provide.
produces: Tool coverage by language and framework

smes.name: API Security
smes.owns: Authentication and authorisation at API edges, schema governance, rate limiting and abuse protection.
never_assume: That the API inventory is complete. Undocumented and legacy endpoints are the ones that get exploited.
That authorisation is checked per object. Broken object-level authorisation is the most common serious API flaw and passes most testing.
That the gateway sees every call. Internal callers frequently bypass it.
That rate limits are set from measured traffic. Estimated limits either throttle real customers or stop nothing.

must_ask.q: How was the API inventory derived - from design, or from observed traffic?
Is authorisation checked at object level, and how was that verified?
Which callers reach these APIs without passing the gateway?

escalate_when: API authorisation depends on a decision point the IAM domain owns.
An API exposes data whose classification the data domain must set.
Public exposure needs edge protection the infrastructure domain owns.

smes.name: Software Supply-Chain Security
smes.owns: SLSA-style build assurance, SBOM, artefact signing and provenance from commit to runtime.
never_assume: That an assurance level claimed can be evidenced. Ask what the pipeline itself produces, and whether the build infrastructure is attested.
That an SBOM is complete. Transitive and build-time dependencies are routinely missing.
That signing implies verification. An artefact signed but never verified at admission proves nothing.
That first-party provenance covers the risk. Most supply-chain compromise arrives through dependencies.

must_ask.q: Is the build infrastructure itself attested, or does the provenance chain terminate at an unverified builder?
What proportion of dependencies, including transitive, carry verifiable provenance?
Where is signature verification enforced, and in which environments?

escalate_when: Admission control enforcement is owned by the infrastructure or platform domain.
A provenance claim is being relied on as evidence by the GRC domain.
A dependency is supplied by a third party whose materiality GRC must assess.
produces: Provenance chain from commit to admission

smes.name: Threat Modelling
smes.owns: Threat modelling as a continuing programme rather than a one-off event, and the traceability from threat to control.
never_assume: That a threat model exists because a workshop happened. Ask when it was last updated against the current design.
That the model covers the deployment, not just the application. Most stop at the application boundary and miss the pipeline and the platform.
That identified threats have controls. Ask which threats were accepted and by whom.
That the model was done by people who knew the attack. A model built only by the build team reproduces its blind spots.

must_ask.q: When was the threat model last updated against the design as it now stands?
Which identified threats have no control, and who accepted each?
Does the model cover the pipeline and the platform, or only the application?

escalate_when: A threat's control lives in another domain.
The threat model should be the input to detection content the SecOps domain owns.
An offensive-security exercise should validate a threat this model identified.

smes.name: Product Security
smes.owns: Security as a property of the product lifecycle and roadmap rather than a gate applied to it.
never_assume: That security work is on the roadmap because it is in the backlog. Ask what is committed to a release.
That customer-facing security commitments are known to engineering. Contractual commitments are often made in sales and never land in a backlog.
That security debt is visible to the people prioritising. It usually sits in a different register from product debt.
That there is a route to tell customers about a vulnerability. Ask who writes it and who approves it.

must_ask.q: What security work is committed to a named release, as opposed to sitting in the backlog?
What security commitments have been made to customers contractually?
What is the process for notifying customers of a vulnerability in this product?

escalate_when: A customer commitment cannot be met by the current architecture.
Vulnerability disclosure needs a coordinated route the offensive-security domain owns.
